lessons.title: Roles in modern IT teams
objectives: Name the common entry-level roles in software and IT
Describe how engineers, analysts, QA, IT support and data roles collaborate
intro: Modern IT teams are built from specialised roles that hand work to each other. A typical product team might include frontend engineers (user interface), backend engineers (servers and data), QA engineers (testing), data analysts (metrics), IT support (access and hardware) and a product manager (decides what to build). Entry-level jobs usually sit inside one of these roles, but you will talk to all of them every week.
Understanding this map helps you choose a first role and explains why nearly every job posting asks for communication skills alongside technical ones: your daily work is translating between roles.
keyPoints: Entry-level roles include junior developer, QA/test engineer, IT/support engineer, data analyst and DevOps associate.
Work flows in cycles: plan → build → test → release → monitor → fix.
Each role owns a different quality attribute: speed, correctness, cost, security or usability.
Communication is part of the job, not a bonus skill.
practice: Write three sentences describing what a junior backend engineer does on a normal Tuesday.

lessons.title: Reading job descriptions without panic
objectives: Decode common job-description phrasing into concrete skills
intro: Job descriptions are marketing documents written by several people. "1–3 years experience" on an entry-level role usually means "you should have built a few real projects". "Familiarity with the MERN stack" means MongoDB, Express, React and Node — a checklist you can map to your learning plan.

A practical method: list every technology mentioned, mark each as (a) already used by you in a project, (b) learned but not in a project, (c) untouched. Apply where (a) and (b) are at least a third of the list.
keyPoints: Translate vague phrases into specific technologies and skills.
Compare your project evidence against the list, not your feelings.
Apply when you match ~1/3 of the list — "requirements" are often wish-lists.
Track every application; rejection rates are high and impersonal for everyone.
practice: Find one real junior-role description, extract its skill list, and mark each item a/b/c as above.

lessons.title: Setting up a sustainable study routine
objectives: Build a realistic weekly study timetable you can keep
Use deliberate practice instead of passive video watching
intro: Consistency beats intensity. One hour of focused building most days outperforms a nine-hour Sunday cram session, because skills consolidate between sessions. Plan around your real life: pick fixed slots, put them in a calendar, and protect them.

Deliberate practice means: attempt something slightly beyond your comfort zone, struggle productively, then check yourself (run the tests, compare with the official docs, ask for review). Re-watching tutorials feels productive but rarely builds skill on its own.
keyPoints: Short, frequent sessions beat long, rare ones.
Every session should include building or answering — not only watching.
Track hours so progress is visible on hard weeks.
Rest is part of practice; sleep is when memory consolidates.
practice: Write a 7-day timetable with at least 5 study blocks, each with a concrete task.

lessons.title: Your first portfolio: what recruiters actually look at
objectives: Describe what makes a beginner project worth showing
Plan a README that explains your project clearly
intro: Recruiters viewing junior portfolios spend under a minute per candidate on first pass. They look for: does it run, is there a README, does the code look organised, was this copied from a tutorial or extended with your own ideas? One well-explained project with a clear README beats five tutorial clones.
A strong README answers: what problem does this solve, how do I run it, what did I learn, what would I add next. Screenshots and a live link (or short demo video) help a lot.
keyPoints: One explained project beats five unexplained clones.
README must cover: problem, how to run, learnings, next steps.
Show a live demo or demo video when hosting is hard.
Original extensions to tutorials are fine if you explain your changes.
practice: Take your best project and write the four-section README described above.

lessons.title: Variables, types and your first programs
objectives: Write and run a small program that reads input and prints output
intro: A variable is a named box that holds a value your program can use later. Every value has a type — text (string), whole numbers (integer), decimal numbers (float), true/false (boolean) — and types decide what operations make sense.
The fastest way to learn is to write tiny programs: read a name, print a greeting, add two numbers. The linked Python and JavaScript topics below cover this in depth with runnable examples.
keyPoints: Variables store values under a name; types define allowed operations.
Input arrives as text unless you convert it explicitly.
Print early and often while learning — it is your window into the program.
Use the linked Python/JavaScript topics for full worked examples.
practice: Write a program that asks for two numbers and prints their sum and difference.

lessons.title: Conditions and loops
objectives: Repeat work with for and while loops
intro: Conditions let a program choose between paths; loops let it repeat work without copy-pasting. Together they express almost all procedural logic.
Classic beginner traps: off-by-one errors in loops, using == when you meant =, and infinite while loops whose condition never becomes false.
keyPoints: if/else chooses a path; boolean expressions drive the choice.
for loops suit a known count; while loops suit a condition.
Test loops with 0, 1 and many items.
Every while loop needs a change that eventually ends it.
practice: Print all even numbers from 1 to 20, then all odd numbers from 1 to 20.

lessons.title: Functions and clean structure
objectives: Use parameters and return values correctly
intro: A function is a named, reusable block of logic with inputs (parameters) and an output (return value). Functions keep programs readable as they grow: each should do one understandable job.
Signs a function needs splitting: longer than a screen, needs comments to explain each step, or two call sites need slightly different versions of it.
keyPoints: Functions take parameters, do one job, and return a result.
Name functions as actions: calculateTotal, sendEmail, isValid.
Small focused functions are easier to test and reuse.
Avoid functions that secretly change global state.
practice: Refactor your sum/difference program into functions calculateSum(a,b) and calculateDifference(a,b).

lessons.title: Data structures you will use daily
objectives: Choose between arrays/lists, objects/maps and sets
intro: Almost every program organises data in a handful of structures. Arrays (lists) hold ordered items; objects (maps/dictionaries) hold labelled key→value pairs; sets hold unique values with fast membership tests.
Choosing the right structure makes code both faster and clearer: a set for "have I seen this email before?", a map for "look up user by id", a list for "show tasks in order".
keyPoints: Lists/arrays: ordered, indexed, allow duplicates.
Maps/objects/dicts: key→value lookup.
Sets: uniqueness and fast "contains" checks.
Watch data size: O(n) scans inside big loops get slow.
practice: Write a program that reads words and prints each unique word with how many times it appeared.

lessons.title: HTTP, requests and responses
objectives: Describe what happens when you open a website
Identify methods, status codes and headers
intro: When you visit a URL, your browser sends an HTTP request (method + URL + headers) to a server, which returns a response (status code + headers + body). GET reads data, POST creates it, PUT/PATCH update, DELETE removes.
Status codes group outcomes: 2xx success, 3xx redirect, 4xx your mistake (404 not found, 403 forbidden), 5xx server fault. Debugging web apps is mostly reading these carefully.
keyPoints: Browsers speak HTTP: request in, response out.
Methods encode intent: GET read, POST create, PUT update, DELETE remove.
2xx success · 4xx client error · 5xx server error.
Headers carry metadata like content-type and authorisation.
practice: Open browser dev tools, load any site, and list the requests, methods and status codes you see.

lessons.title: HTML structure and semantics
objectives: Choose semantic elements over generic divs
intro: HTML describes structure and meaning, not appearance. Semantic elements (header, nav, main, article, footer) tell browsers and screen readers what each region is for, improving accessibility and search ranking.
Forms are central to real apps: learn input types, labels tied to inputs, and basic validation attributes.
keyPoints: Semantic HTML aids accessibility and SEO.
Every input should have a matching label.
Headings should nest in order (h1 → h2 → h3).
Validate on the client AND the server.
practice: Build a contact-form page using only semantic HTML, with proper labels and required fields.

lessons.title: CSS layout and responsive design
objectives: Use flexbox and grid for layout
Make a page usable on phones
intro: CSS controls presentation. Flexbox lays items in one dimension (a row or column); grid lays them in two (rows and columns). Between them you can build almost any layout without floats or hacks.
Responsive design means your page works from 320px phones to wide desktops: use relative units (%, rem), media queries, and test in dev tools at multiple widths.
keyPoints: Flexbox for one-dimensional layouts, grid for two-dimensional.
Prefer rem/% over fixed px for anything scalable.
Mobile-first: base styles for small screens, enhance upward.
Test at 320px, 768px and 1280px widths.
practice: Rebuild your contact-form page as a responsive card that looks good at 360px and 1280px.

tracks.name: Software Engineering
tracks.tagline: Design, build and maintain software systems end to end.
overview: Software engineering is the broad discipline of designing, building, testing and maintaining software. A software engineer works across the full stack of concerns — modelling data, writing code, writing tests, reviewing other people’s code and keeping systems running in production.

For beginners it is the safest generalist entry point: the fundamentals (a language, version control, testing, teamwork) transfer to every specialisation, so you can start here and narrow later toward frontend, backend, data or DevOps without restarting.
responsibilities: Translate requirements into small, testable units of work
Write, review and refactor code with clear structure
Debug production issues and improve reliability
Collaborate through version control, code review and estimation
Document decisions so future changes are safe
prerequisites: Comfortable using a computer filesystem and terminal basics
One programming language at beginner level (Python or JavaScript recommended)

modules.title: Code that other people can read

lessons.title: Readable code: naming, formatting, small functions
objectives: Split long functions into single-purpose ones
intro: Readable code is a professional skill, not a taste preference. Most maintenance time is spent reading, so optimise for the reader: descriptive names (isEmailValid, not chk), one level of indentation per block, functions under roughly 30 lines that do one job.
Adopt a formatter (Black for Python, Prettier for JS) and let it remove style debates entirely.
keyPoints: Name things by what they mean, not how they are stored.
Functions should read like a paragraph: one idea.
Automate formatting instead of arguing about it.
Comments explain why, not what.
practice: Take any 40-line function you have written and split it into named steps without changing behaviour.

lessons.title: Version control with Git: branch, commit, merge
intro: Git tracks snapshots of your project. The everyday loop is: create a branch, make small commits with clear messages, open a pull request, address review, merge. Commit early so nothing is lost, and write messages as sentences describing the change ("Fix off-by-one in pagination") rather than "update".
Learn git status, git diff, git log, git branch, git merge and how to undo with git restore before anything fancier.
keyPoints: One logical change per commit.
Commit messages describe the change, not the file.
Pull requests are for review, not backup.
git status is your best friend when lost.
practice: Make a repo, commit a file across three branches, merge them, and deliberately create then resolve a conflict.

lessons.title: Reading stack traces and debugging systematically
objectives: Read a stack trace to find the fault line
Use the scientific method when debugging
intro: A stack trace lists the chain of function calls that led to an error — read it looking for the first lines mentioning your own files. Reproduce the bug reliably, form one hypothesis, change one variable, observe. Random fixing wastes hours.
Print debugging works; breakpoints in a real debugger work better because you can inspect live values without editing code.
keyPoints: Find your own code in the stack trace first.
Reproduce bugs on demand before fixing.
Change one thing at a time.
Fix the root cause, not the symptom.
practice: Write a program with a deliberate off-by-one bug, run it, and use the stack trace to locate and fix it.

lessons.title: Unit tests and the AAA pattern
objectives: Cover edge cases, not just happy paths
intro: A unit test checks one small piece of code in isolation. Structure tests as Arrange (set up data), Act (call the function), Assert (check the result). Test edge cases deliberately: empty input, zero, negative numbers, very long strings — that is where bugs live.
Aim for tests that fail for the right reason: if your test passes when the function is broken, the test is worthless.
keyPoints: One behaviour per test, named after the behaviour.
Test edge cases first; they catch more bugs.
Tests that cannot fail are decoration.
Keep tests independent so one failure does not cascade.
practice: Write 5 tests for a function that validates a password, including at least 3 edge cases.

lessons.title: Test-driven development: does it fit you?
objectives: Decide when TDD helps and when it slows you down
intro: Test-driven development means writing a failing test before the code that passes it: red (test fails), green (minimal code to pass), refactor (clean up). It produces well-tested code and clear design feedback, but can feel slow on exploratory work.
Even if you do not practice strict TDD, writing tests right after a feature works well. Choose per task, not by ideology.
keyPoints: TDD cycle: failing test → minimal pass → refactor.
Good for well-specified logic; awkward for UI exploration.
Always write tests eventually — timing is the choice.
practice: Implement a roman-numeral converter using strict red–green–refactor for 3 functions.

lessons.title: Designing REST APIs that age well
objectives: Version APIs and handle errors uniformly
intro: A REST API exposes resources (nouns) with standard verbs: GET /orders, POST /orders, GET /orders/:id. Consistency matters more than cleverness — the same pagination, error and naming conventions everywhere. Plan for change: version the API and never break existing clients silently.
Return proper status codes and a uniform error body so clients can react programmatically.
keyPoints: Resources are nouns; HTTP methods are verbs.
Uniform errors, pagination and auth across endpoints.
Version from day one; breaking changes need a new version.
Validate input at the boundary.
practice: Design (on paper) the endpoints for a task-tracker API including pagination and error shapes.

lessons.title: Databases: schema design and safe migrations
objectives: Normalise tables to avoid duplicate data
intro: Relational databases keep data consistent with schemas, keys and constraints. Model entities and relationships properly (one customer, many orders) and let the database enforce rules with foreign keys and unique constraints rather than trusting application code alone.
Migrations are versioned schema changes; write them so they can run on live data and, where possible, be reversed.
keyPoints: Foreign keys and constraints beat application-only checks.
One fact stored in one place (normalisation).
Migrations are code: review and test them.
Index the columns you filter and sort by.
practice: Design a schema for a library system (members, books, loans) in SQL and write the CREATE statements.

lessons.title: Performance: measure before optimising
objectives: Profile code to find real bottlenecks
Apply complexity reasoning to hot paths
intro: Performance work starts with measurement, not intuition. Profile to find which function consumes time, optimise that, then measure again — the bottleneck usually moves somewhere surprising. Reason about complexity to avoid accidental quadratic loops over large data.
keyPoints: Profile first; optimise second; re-measure always.
Nested loops over large inputs are the usual suspects.
Caching adds complexity — add it only after measurement.
practice: Take an O(n²) function, rewrite it with a hash map, and benchmark both on 100k items.

lessons.title: How coding interviews are actually run
objectives: Handle the "what would you improve" follow-up
intro: Most coding interviews are collaborative problem-solving: you think out loud, write code, test it, then discuss trade-offs. Interviewers grade communication as heavily as correctness — an incomplete solution explained clearly often beats a silent complete one.
Always narrate: restate the problem, state assumptions, describe your approach before typing, then test with an example.
keyPoints: Restate, plan, then code — never type silently.
Talk through edge cases and complexity.
The follow-up tests depth: discuss trade-offs honestly.
Practice on a plain editor, not only a full IDE.
practice: Record yourself solving a two-sum style problem out loud in 15 minutes.

lessons.title: Portfolio and GitHub hygiene for applications
objectives: Curate a profile that shows your best work
Write project READMEs that sell your thinking
intro: Recruiters check your GitHub: pinned repositories should be your best 3–6 projects, each with a clear README, screenshots and recent commits. Hide abandoned tutorial clones. Contribution graphs matter far less than the quality of a few pinned projects.
keyPoints: Pin your best 3–6 repos; hide the rest.
README: problem, stack, how to run, screenshots, learnings.
Recent, incremental commits show real workflow.
A short demo video in the README helps a lot.
practice: Pin your three best projects and rewrite their READMEs using the four-section structure.

projects.title: Personal expense tracker (CLI or web)
projects.description: Track daily expenses, categorise them, and report monthly totals.
steps: Persist to a file or SQLite

projects.title: URL shortener service
projects.description: Shorten long URLs, redirect, and show click counts.

interview.q: What is the difference between an array and a linked list?
interview.a: Arrays store items contiguously with O(1) index access but costly mid-insertion; linked lists store nodes with pointers, giving cheap insertion once at a node but O(n) access.

interview.q: What does "idempotent" mean for an API?
interview.a: An operation is idempotent if repeating it has the same effect as doing it once — PUT to set a value is idempotent; POST that creates a new record is not.

interview.q: How do you decide a function is too long?
interview.a: When it has multiple reasons to change, needs comments per section, or testing one part requires running all of it — split by responsibility, not line count.

checklist: One language used confidently in at least two projects
Git workflow with branches and pull requests understood
Unit tests written for your own code, not only course code
One REST API built and documented
Resume reviewed by a human; GitHub profile curated
Can solve easy algorithm problems while talking through them

tracks.name: Frontend Development
tracks.tagline: Build the interfaces people actually touch.
overview: Frontend development is everything the user sees and interacts with in a browser: layout, styling, interaction, performance and accessibility. Frontend engineers translate designs into fast, responsive, accessible interfaces and wire them to APIs.

It is the most visual entry point into software: you get immediate feedback on your work, and the required stack (HTML, CSS, JavaScript) runs everywhere with zero setup. Frameworks like React, Vue or Angular come after the fundamentals are solid.
responsibilities: Turn designs and requirements into responsive pages
Optimise load time and runtime performance
Write reusable components and maintain design systems
prerequisites: Eye for detail and patience with browser quirks

lessons.title: Semantic HTML and accessibility essentials
objectives: Add alt text, labels and focus states correctly
intro: Accessibility is not optional polish — many people experience some form of disability, and semantic HTML gives you most of the solution for free. Use button for actions and a for links, label every input, keep headings in order, and provide alt text that describes the image’s purpose.
Keyboard navigation is the quick test: unplug your mouse and Tab through the page. If you cannot reach and trigger every control, something is broken.
keyPoints: Semantics first; ARIA only to fill real gaps.
Every input needs a label; every image needs meaningful alt.
Visible focus styles are essential, not ugly.
Test with keyboard-only navigation every session.
practice: Take any page you built and make it fully usable with keyboard only.

lessons.title: Responsive layout with grid and flexbox
objectives: Build a layout that adapts from 320px to 1920px
Choose grid vs flexbox per section
intro: Grid handles two-dimensional layout (page shells, card galleries); flexbox handles one-dimensional flow (nav bars, toolbars). Real pages combine both: grid for the page, flexbox inside components.
Start from the small screen: define the phone layout first, then add media queries for tablets and desktops. This avoids the trap of removing desktop features downwards.
keyPoints: Grid = rows + columns; flexbox = one axis.
Mobile-first media queries: min-width upward.
minmax() and auto-fit make responsive galleries without extra breakpoints.
Use relative units (rem, %, vw) for anything scalable.
practice: Build a responsive gallery: 1 column on phones, 2 on tablets, 4 on desktop — no horizontal scroll.

lessons.title: DOM manipulation and events in JavaScript
objectives: Handle user events and form input
intro: The DOM is your page as a tree of objects JavaScript can read and change. querySelector finds elements; textContent and classList change them; addEventListener reacts to clicks, input and key presses. Use event delegation for dynamic lists.
Forms are central: read values, validate before submit, prevent the default reload, and give clear inline error messages tied to the offending input.
keyPoints: querySelector / querySelectorAll to select.
Prefer event delegation on containers for dynamic content.
preventDefault() stops page reloads on submit.
Show validation errors next to the input, in text.
practice: Build a todo list: add, toggle-complete and delete items using only DOM APIs — no framework.

lessons.title: Thinking in components
objectives: Split a page into reusable components
intro: Component frameworks (React, Vue, Svelte) treat UI as functions of state: given the same data, the same interface appears. Split UI by responsibility — a Card, a NavBar, a LoginForm — each owning its markup, styles and behaviour.
Keep state as low as possible: only lift it up when two siblings genuinely need it. Prop-drilling through five layers usually signals a missing context or store.
keyPoints: One component = one responsibility.
State lives at the lowest common ancestor that needs it.
Props flow down; events flow up.
Extract components when markup repeats, not before.
practice: Rebuild your todo list as a component tree with at least three components.

lessons.title: Measuring and fixing web performance
objectives: Use Core Web Vitals to find real problems
Apply targeted fixes (lazy loading, code splitting)
intro: Frontend performance has three user-facing metrics: LCP (how fast the main content appears), INP (how fast it responds to input) and CLS (how much the layout jumps). Measure with Lighthouse and real-user monitoring, then fix the biggest offender first — usually images, blocking scripts or heavy hydration.
keyPoints: Measure Core Web Vitals before optimising.
Compress and lazy-load images; serve modern formats.
Code-split so users download only what the page needs.
Debounce expensive handlers; avoid layout thrash.
practice: Audit any site with Lighthouse, list its top three issues, and fix one on your own project.

lessons.title: CSS and JS interview questions you will actually face
objectives: Explain the cascade, specificity and the box model
Answer common JS questions with examples
intro: Frontend interviews mix live coding (build a component or fix CSS) with conceptual questions. Be ready to explain: the box model and box-sizing, cascade and specificity, event bubbling and delegation, closures, the event loop, and the difference between == and ===.
For take-home tasks: read requirements twice, ship something working, then polish README and tests. Reviewers value clarity over feature count.
keyPoints: Box model, specificity, cascade — explain with examples.
Closures and the event loop appear constantly.
Take-homes: working beats exhaustive; document trade-offs.
Talk through your UI decisions while coding.
practice: Answer "explain event delegation" out loud in under two minutes, with a code example.

projects.title: Responsive portfolio website
projects.description: A personal portfolio with projects section, contact form and dark mode, fully responsive.
steps: Add theme toggle and form validation
Deploy and link from your résumé

projects.title: Weather dashboard consuming a public API
projects.description: Search a city, show current weather and a 5-day forecast with loading and error states.
steps: Read the API docs and get a key

interview.q: Explain the CSS box model and box-sizing.
interview.a: Every element is a box of content, padding, border and margin. box-sizing: border-box makes width include padding and border, matching how designers usually specify sizes.

interview.q: What is event delegation?
interview.a: Listening on a common ancestor instead of each child; events bubble up, so one handler can manage all children — essential for dynamic lists.

interview.q: Difference between == and ===?
interview.a: == compares after type coercion ("" == 0 is true); === compares value and type with no coercion. Prefer ===.

checklist: Semantic, accessible HTML in every project
One framework used in at least one real project
Comfortable using dev tools to debug CSS and JS

tracks.name: Backend Development
tracks.tagline: Servers, APIs, databases — the machinery behind the screen.
overview: Backend development powers everything the browser asks for: APIs, business logic, data storage, authentication and integrations. Backend engineers design endpoints, model data, keep systems fast and secure, and make sure the app still works when a thousand users arrive at once.
A practical entry path: pick one language (Python, JavaScript/Node, Go or Java), learn HTTP and SQL deeply, build a few CRUD APIs with authentication, then add testing and deployment.
prerequisites: Basic SQL (see the SQL language path)

lessons.title: Request to response: what a server actually does
objectives: Trace a request through routing, handler and response
Return JSON with correct status codes
intro: A web server listens on a port, matches each incoming request to a route, runs a handler function, and returns a response — usually JSON. The handler reads the request (path, query, body, headers), does work (query the database, compute), and returns a status code plus body.
Status codes are part of your API contract: 200 for success, 201 for created, 400 for bad input, 401/403 for auth problems, 404 for missing, 500 for your bug.
keyPoints: Route → handler → response is the core loop.
Return meaningful status codes, not always 200.
JSON is the default data format for web APIs.
Validate input at the boundary; never trust the client.
practice: Build an API with one GET endpoint that returns a hard-coded list of users as JSON.

lessons.title: CRUD APIs with a real database
objectives: Map HTTP verbs and status codes to CRUD correctly
intro: CRUD (Create, Read, Update, Delete) maps neatly onto HTTP: POST creates (201), GET reads (200), PUT/PATCH updates (200), DELETE removes (204). Pair each with a database table and you have the backbone of most apps.
Always validate the body before writing to the database, use parameterised queries to prevent SQL injection, and return 404 for resources that do not exist rather than an empty success.
keyPoints: POST 201 · GET 200 · DELETE 204 is a sane convention.
Parameterised queries prevent SQL injection.
Validate every field before it reaches the database.
Return 404 for missing resources.
practice: Build a notes API (create, list, get one, update, delete) backed by SQLite or Postgres.

lessons.title: Authentication without rolling your own crypto
objectives: Explain password hashing and why plain text is unacceptable
Implement session or token login safely
intro: Store passwords only as hashes made with a slow, salted algorithm (bcrypt, scrypt, argon2) — never plain text, never fast hashes like bare SHA-256. On login, hash the attempt and compare.
Choose sessions (server-side state in a cookie) or tokens (JWT or opaque tokens returned by a login endpoint). Sessions are simpler to revoke; make cookies HttpOnly and Secure.
keyPoints: Hash with bcrypt/scrypt/argon2 + per-user salt.
Use established libraries; never invent crypto.
HttpOnly, Secure cookies for session tokens.
Rate-limit login endpoints against brute force.
practice: Add signup/login with hashed passwords to your notes API, and protect two endpoints.

lessons.title: Indexes, N+1 queries and caching basics
objectives: Spot and fix N+1 query patterns
Add indexes for hot query paths
intro: The most common backend performance bug is the N+1 query: loading a list, then making one extra query per row. Fix it with JOINs or batch loading. The second most common is missing indexes — check EXPLAIN before assuming a query is "just slow".
Caching (in-memory or Redis) helps read-heavy endpoints, but adds staleness bugs: cache deliberately, with explicit expiry.
keyPoints: N+1 queries: one list query + one per item — fix with JOINs.
Index columns used in WHERE, JOIN and ORDER BY.
Measure with EXPLAIN, not guesses.
Caching trades staleness for speed — be explicit.
practice: Take a slow list endpoint, log its queries, and reduce the query count to a constant.

lessons.title: Message queues, idempotency and eventual consistency
objectives: Describe when a queue beats a direct call
intro: Queues decouple producers from consumers so slow or flaky work (emails, image processing) cannot take down the request path. The catch: messages can arrive twice or out of order, so consumers must be idempotent — applying the same message twice has the same effect as once.
keyPoints: Queues absorb bursts and isolate failures.
At-least-once delivery means idempotent consumers.
Use idempotency keys for unsafe operations.
Eventual consistency is a product decision, not only a technical one.
practice: Design an email-sending flow with a queue, retries and deduplication — on paper.

lessons.title: System design for juniors and SQL interviews
objectives: Write complex SQL under time pressure
intro: Junior system design questions are deliberately small ("design a URL shortener"): clarify requirements, propose the data model, sketch the API, note one bottleneck and how you would scale it. Depth on one design beats shallow talk of five technologies.
SQL interviews test joins, aggregation and window functions. Practice SELECT with GROUP BY, HAVING and simple window functions until writing them is mechanical.
keyPoints: Clarify → data model → API → bottleneck → scale.
Practice joins, GROUP BY, HAVING, window functions.
Explain trade-offs out loud; interviewers want reasoning.
Ask clarifying questions — it is scored positively.
practice: Time yourself designing a URL shortener in 15 minutes, speaking aloud.

projects.title: Task management API
projects.description: REST API for projects and tasks with user auth, filtering and pagination.

projects.title: Rate-limited URL shortener API
projects.description: Shorten URLs, redirect with click counting, rate-limit by API key.

interview.q: What is the N+1 query problem?
interview.a: Loading a list of items and then issuing one separate query per item inside a loop. Fix by joining or batch-loading so the total query count is constant.

interview.q: Sessions vs JWT — when would you pick each?
interview.a: Sessions are simple to revoke (delete server state) and fit monoliths; JWTs are stateless and fit distributed services but need rotation and careful revocation design.

interview.q: How do you prevent SQL injection?
interview.a: Use parameterised queries / prepared statements from your driver or ORM; never concatenate user input into SQL strings.

checklist: One CRUD API with auth, deployed somewhere
Password hashing done with a real library
Tests covering happy path and error cases
Can explain one design trade-off from your own project

tracks.name: Full-Stack Development
tracks.tagline: Own a feature from database table to rendered pixel.
overview: Full-stack developers work across both the frontend and backend of an application: designing the data model and API, then building the interface that uses them. In small teams and startups this breadth is essential; in larger organisations full-stack roles still exist but tend to lean toward one side.

The learning path combines the frontend and backend tracks. The advantage is understanding the whole request cycle; the risk is depthlessness — mitigate it by going deep on one side first, whichever you enjoy more.
responsibilities: Build features across API and UI layers
Design data models that fit the product
Write tests on both sides of the stack
Deploy and monitor the whole application
prerequisites: Willingness to work in both browser and server tooling

soft: Owning a feature end to end

lessons.title: Thinking in full request cycles
objectives: Trace a full-stack request from click to database and back
Identify where each layer’s responsibility ends
intro: A full-stack feature is one continuous cycle: the UI captures intent, the frontend validates and sends an HTTP request, the backend authorises, validates and queries the database, then serialises a response the UI renders. Being able to narrate this cycle for your own project is the single best interview story you can have.
Practise drawing the cycle for any feature you build: boxes for UI, API, DB, with the data moving between them labelled.
keyPoints: Trace: UI event → request → handler → DB → response → render.
Each layer validates again — never trust the layer before you.
Auth checks belong at the API, not only the UI.
Draw the cycle; diagrams expose missing steps.
practice: Pick one feature in your project and write out its full request cycle in 6 steps.

lessons.title: Sessions vs tokens across the stack
objectives: Compare session-cookie and token auth flows

lessons.title: Profiling a slow feature across layers
objectives: Measure frontend and backend latency separately

lessons.title: STAR stories from your own projects

projects.title: Blogging platform with auth
projects.description: Users sign up, write posts, edit and delete their own; the public sees all posts.

projects.title: Expense sharing app (Splitwise-lite)
projects.description: Groups, expenses, per-member balances and settlement suggestions.

interview.q: Walk me through what happens when a user submits a login form.
interview.a: The browser POSTs credentials; the server rate-limits, validates format, looks up the user, compares the password hash, then creates a session (Set-Cookie) or returns a token; the client includes it in subsequent requests; the server authorises each request against it.

interview.q: Where should validation live?
interview.a: In the UI for feedback, and always again in the API — the UI can be bypassed with curl, so the server is the authority.

interview.q: How do you keep frontend and backend types in sync?
interview.a: Shared type definitions (TypeScript types or an OpenAPI schema) generated from one source of truth, plus contract tests on critical endpoints.

checklist: One deployed full-stack app with auth
Can trace and explain every request cycle in your project
SQL modelling understood, not only ORM magic
Frontend and backend tests both exist
Comfortable debugging across layers with logs

tracks.name: Data Analytics & Business Intelligence
tracks.tagline: Turn raw data into decisions people can act on.
overview: Data analysts answer questions business people actually have: why did sales drop, which segment churns most, is the new feature working. The day-to-day toolkit is SQL for extracting data, a spreadsheet or Python/R for wrangling and statistics, and a visualisation tool (Power BI, Tableau or Python) for communicating findings.

It is an accessible entry point if you like questions more than code: SQL can be learned in weeks, and analysis quality comes from framing the right question and communicating clearly more than from fancy models.
responsibilities: Translate business questions into data queries
Define metrics and track them over time

modules.title: Questions, data and your first insights

lessons.title: Framing questions the data can actually answer
objectives: Frame a vague business question as an answerable data question
Identify what data you would need
intro: "Is the business doing well?" is not answerable; "did weekly active users grow or shrink over the last quarter, and in which region?" is. Analysts spend their early career learning to sharpen questions like this.
Before touching SQL, write down: the metric, the comparison (vs last month? vs target?), the segment, and the time range. This prevents beautiful analyses of the wrong question.
keyPoints: A good data question names metric, segment, comparison and time range.
Always ask what decision the answer will drive.
Write the question down before writing any query.
Garbage in, garbage out: check data quality first.
practice: Take three vague questions ("are customers happy?", "is marketing working?", "is the app slow?") and rewrite each as an answerable data question.

lessons.title: Advanced SQL: window functions and CTEs
objectives: Write window functions for running totals and rankings
Use CTEs for readable multi-step queries

lessons.title: Presenting findings to stakeholders
objectives: Choose the right chart for the message
intro: You have a dataset and a stakeholder who needs an answer. Lead with the decision, not the method: one slide situation, one slide what the data says, one slide what you recommend, then appendix with method.
Practice the "one-minute summary": if you cannot state the finding in a minute, you have not finished thinking.
keyPoints: Lead with the decision, not the method.
One chart, one message.
State confidence and caveats honestly.
Appendix holds method details; main deck holds the story.
practice: Summarise a real or public dataset’s top three findings in a 3-slide outline.

projects.title: Sales dashboard from a public dataset
projects.description: Load a sales CSV, answer 5 business questions in SQL, and visualise monthly trends.

projects.title: Customer churn analysis
projects.description: Identify which customer segments churn most and why, with evidence.

interview.q: Difference between INNER JOIN and LEFT JOIN?
interview.a: INNER JOIN returns only rows matching in both tables; LEFT JOIN returns all rows from the left table plus matching rows from the right (NULL where no match).

interview.q: What is a window function and when do you use one?
interview.a: A window function computes across a set of rows related to the current row without collapsing them (running totals, rankings, per-segment averages) — unlike GROUP BY which aggregates many rows into one.

interview.q: How would you explain a p-value to a non-technical manager?
interview.a: It is the probability of seeing an effect this big in the test data if there were actually no real difference — small p-values mean the result would be surprising under "no effect".

checklist: SQL: joins, GROUP BY, window functions comfortable
Can explain a metric definition precisely
One written analysis with a clear recommendation

tracks.name: AI Application Development & Automation
tracks.tagline: Build practical products on top of AI models and automation.
overview: This track sits between raw ML engineering and product development: building applications that call existing AI models (including large language models), add retrieval from your own data, and automate workflows with reliable guardrails. It needs strong software engineering more than maths.
Demand grew with accessible LLM APIs. Entry is realistic for developers who already write APIs and want to add AI features responsibly — with evaluation, cost control and safety in mind.
responsibilities: Integrate AI model APIs into products
Add guardrails, logging and cost controls
Automate business workflows end to end
prerequisites: Comfort with HTTP APIs and JSON

interview.q: How do you prevent a chatbot from inventing facts?
interview.a: Ground it with retrieval over trusted documents, require citations, restrict answers to retrieved context, and measure hallucination rate on a fixed test set.

interview.q: How do you control cost for an LLM feature?
interview.a: Cap input/output tokens, cache repeated prompts, use smaller models for simple subtasks, and monitor spend per request with alerts.

tracks.name: Cybersecurity
tracks.tagline: Defend systems, find weaknesses, respond to incidents.
overview: Cybersecurity protects the confidentiality, integrity and availability of systems and data. Roles range from defensive (security operations, monitoring, hardening) to offensive (penetration testing) to governance (risk, compliance).

Entry often comes via IT support or networking roles plus self-study and labs; certifications (Security+, CySA+) help open doors. Expect continuous learning. This platform teaches defensive fundamentals and does not teach attacking systems you do not own.
responsibilities: Run vulnerability scans and track remediation
Respond to incidents and document them
prerequisites: Systems or IT support experience helps

steps: Verify with scans on your lab

interview.q: Explain the difference between authentication and authorisation.
interview.a: Authentication verifies who you are; authorisation decides what that identity may do. They are separate layers and both must be enforced.

interview.q: What is the first step in incident response?
interview.a: Preparation, then detection and analysis: confirm the alert is real, scope it, and preserve evidence before containment.

interview.q: How does MFA resist password theft?
interview.a: A stolen password alone is insufficient; the attacker also needs the second factor (phone app, hardware key), much harder to phish at scale.

checklist: Isolated lab built and used regularly

tracks.name: Cloud Computing
tracks.tagline: Run reliable systems on rented infrastructure — smartly.
overview: Cloud computing means running workloads on someone else’s computers, metered by usage. Cloud engineers design how applications use compute, storage and networking in the cloud, keeping them available and cost-effective. It underpins nearly every modern software team.

A practical entry: pick one provider (AWS, Azure or GCP), get hands-on with free tiers, and automate with infrastructure-as-code. Certifications help pass résumé screens; projects prove you can actually build.
responsibilities: Design for high availability and recovery
Support developers with environments and pipelines

interview.q: What is the shared responsibility model?
interview.a: The provider secures the cloud infrastructure; you secure what you put in it — configs, data, access controls. Misunderstanding this causes most cloud breaches.

interview.q: Difference between scalability and elasticity?
interview.a: Scalability is handling growth; elasticity is automatic scaling up AND down with demand to control cost.

interview.q: What is high availability?
interview.a: Designing so the system keeps working when components fail, usually by removing single points of failure and running across multiple zones.

checklist: Backups tested with a restore drill

tracks.name: DevOps & Platform Engineering
tracks.tagline: Automate the path from code to production, safely.
overview: DevOps joins development and operations: building the pipelines, environments and tooling that let teams ship software quickly and reliably. Platform engineering extends this into internal products that other developers self-serve.

The field rewards breadth: scripting, Linux, networking, cloud and developer empathy. An entry path is through backend, IT support or QA roles while picking up CI/CD, containers and infrastructure-as-code on the side.
responsibilities: Improve reliability with monitoring and on-call practices

interview.q: What is infrastructure as code and why does it matter?
interview.a: Defining infrastructure in version-controlled files instead of clicking in a console: reproducible, reviewable, diffable environments.

interview.q: Blue-green vs canary deployments?
interview.a: Blue-green switches all traffic to a new environment at once (fast rollback, needs double capacity); canary shifts traffic gradually (safer, slower).

interview.q: What makes a good alert?
interview.a: It is actionable, tied to a user-facing problem, has a documented response, and fires rarely enough that people still pay attention.

tracks.name: Software Testing & QA Automation
tracks.tagline: Prove software works — and keep proving it automatically.
overview: QA engineers protect users by finding defects before release and building automation that catches regressions forever. Modern QA blends manual exploratory testing with coded automation, and increasingly shifts left into design and requirements reviews.
It is one of the most accessible software entries: strong analytical thinking plus one scripting language and a test framework can qualify you for junior roles, especially with domain curiosity.
responsibilities: Build and maintain automated test suites

interview.q: What is exploratory testing?
interview.a: Simultaneous learning, design and execution of tests without a fixed script — testers use domain knowledge and curiosity to find issues scripted tests miss.

interview.q: How do you handle a flaky test?
interview.a: Quarantine it so it blocks no one, reproduce the root cause (timing, data, order dependence), fix properly, and track flake rate as a metric.

interview.q: What belongs in a good bug report?
interview.a: Clear title, environment/version, exact steps to reproduce, expected vs actual, severity, and evidence (logs/screenshots).

tracks.name: Database Development & Data Engineering
tracks.tagline: Design the pipelines and stores that make analytics possible.
overview: Data engineers build and maintain the systems that collect, store, transform and serve data: warehouses, pipelines, orchestration and quality checks. Analysts and ML engineers are your customers; reliability and correctness are your product.

A realistic entry comes from backend or analytics backgrounds: strong SQL plus Python, then batch/stream processing tools (dbt, Airflow, Spark) and warehouse platforms (Snowflake, BigQuery, Redshift).

interview.q: Star schema vs snowflake schema?
interview.a: Star schema keeps dimension tables denormalised for simple, fast queries; snowflake normalises dimensions to save space at the cost of more joins.

interview.q: What is idempotency in pipelines?
interview.a: Re-running a pipeline produces the same result — achieved by deterministic transformations and upserts keyed on stable identifiers.

interview.q: How do you ensure data quality?
interview.a: Tests on rows, ranges and relationships (e.g. dbt tests), freshness checks, anomaly detection, and clear ownership when data breaks.

tracks.tagline: Ship apps people carry in their pockets.
overview: Mobile developers build applications for phones and tablets, either natively (Swift/Kotlin) or cross-platform (Flutter, React Native). Mobile work blends UI craft with platform constraints: battery, screen sizes, offline states and strict app-store review.

Entry paths differ: native requires learning a platform’s language and tooling; cross-platform lets web developers move faster with existing JavaScript skills. Both need real published (or well-tested) projects to show.
prerequisites: Either Swift/Kotlin basics or JavaScript for cross-platform

interview.q: Native vs cross-platform — when which?
interview.a: Native for maximum platform fidelity/performance; cross-platform (Flutter/RN) for speed and shared code across iOS/Android, with some trade-offs in deep platform integration.

interview.q: How do you handle app state?
interview.a: With a predictable pattern (provider, bloc, Redux-like store) separating UI state from business logic, so screens are testable and debuggable.

interview.q: What causes app store rejections?
interview.a: Crashes on review, broken links, misleading metadata, privacy violations (missing permission explanations), and policy non-compliance around payments or content.

tracks.tagline: Keep people and systems connected and working.
overview: IT support and networking professionals are the backbone of every organisation: they resolve user issues, manage hardware and accounts, and keep networks running. It is the most common on-ramp into a tech career, with clear progression into sysadmin, security or cloud roles.

Core skills are troubleshooting method, networking fundamentals (TCP/IP, DNS, DHCP), ticketing discipline and communication under pressure. Certifications like CompTIA A+ and Network+ are recognised entry credentials.
responsibilities: Resolve user tickets promptly and clearly

interview.q: User says "the internet is down" — first steps?
interview.a: Confirm scope (one user or many), check physical links and IP config, test name resolution vs connectivity, then escalate with findings if it is network-wide.

interview.q: What is DNS and what fails when it breaks?
interview.a: The system translating domain names to IP addresses; when it fails, sites "stop working" by name even though raw IP connectivity may still work.

interview.q: How do you prioritise a full ticket queue?
interview.a: By impact and urgency: many users blocked > one user blocked > individual annoyance; communicate ETAs so nobody is surprised.

tracks.name: UI/UX & Product Design
tracks.tagline: Design products that are usable, useful and desirable.
overview: Product designers own how a product looks, feels and flows: research, information architecture, interaction design, visual design and prototyping. UX is the structure and usability; UI is the visual layer; real products need both.

A portfolio of end-to-end case studies matters far more than degrees: show the problem, your research, iterations with rationale, and the shipped outcome. Designers who can also implement (HTML/CSS, basic front-end) collaborate better with engineers.

Collaborate daily with engineering and product

interview.q: Walk me through a case study.
interview.a: Problem and constraints → research insights → design decisions and alternatives considered → validation results → shipped outcome and learnings.

interview.q: How do you handle disagreement with an engineer?
interview.a: Understand the constraint first, then iterate on the design within it; use data or a quick test to break ties instead of authority.

interview.q: What makes a good design system?
interview.a: Consistent tokens and components, clear documentation, contribution rules, and adoption support — a product, not a static file.

overview: Business analysts translate business goals into requirements engineers can build, and keep stakeholders aligned. Product operations supports the product org itself: process, data, tooling and rituals that help product teams move faster.

This is a strong path for communicators who like structure and problem framing more than coding — though technical literacy dramatically increases effectiveness. Domain expertise (finance, healthcare, retail) compounds over time.

interview.q: How do you handle conflicting stakeholder priorities?
interview.a: Surface the conflict with data on goals/impact, facilitate a trade-off discussion against agreed criteria, and document the decision with rationale.

interview.q: What makes a good user story?
interview.a: A clear user/value framing plus testable acceptance criteria — "As a X, I want Y so that Z" with conditions of satisfaction everyone can verify.

interview.q: How do you know requirements are complete?
interview.a: They are testable, unambiguous to developers, cover edge cases and errors, and have sign-off from the people accountable for the outcome.

tracks.tagline: Teach computers to learn patterns from data.
overview: Machine learning engineers build systems that improve from data: predicting churn, ranking search results, detecting fraud, transcribing speech. The role blends software engineering with statistics and careful experiment design.

Entry is demanding on maths (linear algebra, probability, calculus basics) and Python, but realistic through data analytics or backend routes plus focused ML study. Portfolios of well-evaluated models matter more than certificates.

projects.title: Tabular prediction with honest evaluation
projects.description: Pick a public tabular dataset; build a classifier with a proper held-out test set and a short write-up.

interview.q: What is overfitting and how do you detect it?
interview.a: The model memorises training noise instead of general patterns; detected when training performance is much better than validation/test performance on unseen data.

interview.q: Why split data into train/validation/test?
interview.a: Train fits the model, validation guides choices (hyperparameters, model selection), and a held-out test estimates real-world performance once — keeping each role separate avoids optimistic bias.

interview.q: Precision vs recall — when does each matter?
interview.a: Precision: of flagged items, how many were right (matters when false alarms are costly). Recall: of real positives, how many were caught (matters when misses are costly, e.g. disease screening).

checklist: One end-to-end model with honest held-out evaluation
Can explain overfitting and validation clearly
